object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A formal response to a detected problem affecting one or more services. Identified by incident number and tracked through states from triage to closure.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A measure of blast radius and technical impact of an incident, ranging from SEV1 (complete outage) to SEV4 (cosmetic degradation).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A measure of customer urgency based on business impact, affected parties, SLA obligations, and customer promises. Independent from severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4... Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current state of an incident in its lifecycle: triage (initial assessment), declared (active response), mitigated (temporary fix applied), resolved (fix deployed), or closed (complete).

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform that something may be wrong. Can be automated from monitoring systems or manually created by engineers.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, assigned by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support request or report of a problem, tracked in a separate system from incidents.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a ticket, from the support system.

object_types.name: Service

ambiguities.description: Team identification scheme unclear. Referred to as owning services and having team members, but no specific identifier is stated. The model assumes a team_id reference mode, but stakeholders may use team name or code. Should clarify whether teams are identified by name (unique like services) or by an internal ID.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Person identification scheme unclear. The transcript refers to an incident commander as 'one person, named' but does not specify how persons are uniquely identified. Should clarify whether person identification is by employee ID, name, email, or another scheme.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Commander assignment timing is state-dependent. The model currently allows a commander on any Incident, but the rule is that a commander is mandatory only if the Incident is in the 'declared' state (or post-declared states), and forbidden if in 'triage'. The subset constraint on 'Declared Incident commanded by Person' attempts to capture this, but it depends on a business rule about which states constitute 'declared'. Should clarify whether the subset constraint is correctly applied or if a more explicit state machine constraint is needed.

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage... A commander is assigned when it's declared... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Temporal aspect of severity and priority changes not modeled. Stakeholders mention that severity and priority can change during the incident lifecycle and that the timeline tracks these as events. The current model captures the current values only. Should clarify whether historical severity/priority changes need to be stored in the model or if they are handled solely through timeline events (outside the conceptual model).

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident?... Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected... I'll model the current one and note that changes exist in the timeline.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate chain resolution logic not formally captured. Stakeholders state that duplicate chains should not exist (e.g., if C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point to A), but the acyclic ring constraint alone does not enforce transitive closure or path compression. The rule 'a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything' is stated informally but not explicitly captured. Should clarify whether a constraint is needed to formalize that a primary Incident has no outgoing duplicate relationships.

source_references.excerpt: If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. When we roll up incident counts we only follow one hop, so a chain undercounts... The rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Alert and Ticket distinction from business perspective not fully clarified. Both are origins for an incident, but the transcript does not clearly define whether an Alert and a Ticket can refer to the same underlying event, or whether they are always disjoint. Should clarify: can a single real-world outage result in both an Alert being fired AND a Ticket being created, and if so, are these treated as separate origin facts on the same Incident, or is there a deeper relationship between Alert and Ticket entities?

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

ambiguities.description: Scope of 'Incident' definition remains somewhat open. The transcript discusses a contentious classification issue: incidents caused by customer misconfiguration. This decision is explicitly deferred to Ravi (lines 245–251), and the model does not include a cause classification field. However, this means the current model treats such incidents the same as genuine reliability incidents. Should clarify whether the model will eventually include a cause classification, or whether the business intends to leave this as a post-hoc filtering/reporting concern outside the data model.

source_references.excerpt: It's in mean time to resolve, it's in our incident count for the month, it's in the board deck. And it wasn't an incident, it was a support conversation with an incident record attached to it... The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Granularity of Service ownership model unclear. The transcript states 'services are owned by teams' and 'people move', implying a many-to-one relationship. However, it does not address whether service ownership is current-state only or whether historical ownership should be tracked. If a team changes ownership of a service, should the old relationship be retained for audit purposes? Should clarify whether the model represents current ownership only or if effective dates and historical tracking are needed.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Cardinality of Incident-to-Service relationship appears correctly stated as many-to-many (one or more services per incident), but no constraint is captured on the Service side (how many incidents can affect a given service). The assumption is that a service can be affected by many incidents, but this is not explicitly confirmed. Should clarify whether a service's affected-by relationship is bounded in any way.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service?... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.
